docs.title: UiPath Coding Agents Workshop
docs.text:
Build UiPath agents and Maestro orchestrations with coding agents — from installing the tools to shipping a long-running automation.

Training Environment

Log in at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs using tenant CodingAgentsPractice.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
This workshop takes you from zero to building real automation with coding agents. You start by setting up the uip CLI and UiPath skills, then build agents and orchestrations — letting a coding agent like Claude Code do the heavy lifting while you stay in control.

The course has two parts:

Part 1 · Coding Agents — get your environment ready, learn how building UiPath components changes with a coding agent, and build your first agents: a low-code hello-world, a coded agent with context and tools, and a conversational agent.

Part 2 · Agentic Orchestration — build Coded Apps, then orchestrate agents and apps into Maestro solutions: Case Management, BPMN, and Flow.

Agenda — How the hands-on session runs, in a two-day or a single-day format.

More exercises are being authored and will appear here as they are released.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Coding agent — an AI assistant (e.g., Claude Code) that builds UiPath components from your instructions, using the uip CLI and UiPath skills. UiPath is the automation platform that coding agents operate natively.
  • uip CLI — the command-line interface coding agents use to talk to the UiPath platform.
  • UiPath skills — curated instruction packs that teach a coding agent how to build UiPath automations correctly.
  • Maestro — UiPath's orchestration platform for coordinating humans, robots, and AI agents across long-running processes.

docs.title: Coding Agents + UiPath: Hands-On Session
docs.text:
Build a Coded Agent, an RPA workflow, a Coded App, and a Maestro Flow — all from your coding agent, all wired into one recruitment pipeline.

Here is our plan for this session:

  1. Get the mental model for coding agents, skills, tools, and plugins — see What's a Coding Agent?.
  2. Build a Coded Agent that researches jobs and matches candidates.
  3. Build an RPA workflow that registers those candidates on a web form.
  4. Build a Coded App dashboard that shows the whole pipeline.
  5. Bring the agent and the RPA workflow together in a Maestro Flow that runs the pipeline end to end.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every week a recruiter at a staffing agency does the same four things by hand: search job boards, write a description for each role, read through a candidate pool to find who fits, and register the shortlist in the client's portal. Hours of work, done differently by every recruiter, with nowhere to see where anyone stands.

You'll automate all four — by describing what you want in plain English and letting your coding agent build it. Three components, each handing work to the next through Data Service, and a Maestro Flow that runs them as one process. By the end you'll know exactly when code beats drag-and-drop, and why.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the session you'll have four deployed components talking to each other through Data Service: a Python agent that finds jobs and scores candidates, an XAML workflow that registers each candidate on a website with no API, a React dashboard the recruiter actually uses, and a Maestro Flow that runs the pipeline end to end. You'll have generated all four by prompting a coding agent — not by dragging activities onto a canvas or scaffolding React by hand.

Training Environment

Log in at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs using tenant CodingAgentsPractice.

docs.title: What You'll Build
docs.text:
Four components, all built in the session:

  1. Coded Agent — a Python LangGraph agent that takes a list of job titles, web-searches current openings, generates a structured job description per role, scores a candidate pool against each one, and writes jobs and top-3 matches to Data Service
  2. RPA Workflow — a Studio XAML workflow that reads the matched candidates from Data Service, registers each one on the UiBank web form, and writes the registration status back
  3. Coded App — a React Coded App that reads the Jobs, Job Matches and Candidates entities and presents them to a recruiter, with a button that triggers the agent on demand
  4. Maestro Flow — a UiPath Flow that runs the agent, pauses for a recruiter to approve the shortlist, triggers the RPA registration, and surfaces the result in the app

docs.title: The scenario
docs.text:
A staffing agency is digitizing its recruitment pipeline. Three problems: find jobs, register candidates, and give recruiters a view of everything. Then tie it all together. 01 Coded Agent Searches the web for open jobs, generates structured JDs, matches against a candidate pool. → Writes to Data Service 02 RPA Workflow Reads candidate CSV, registers each one on uibank.uipath.com/register-account. → Writes status back to Data Service 03 Coded App Recruiter dashboard: open jobs, generated descriptions, matched candidates, registration status. → Reads from Data Service 🔗 04 Maestro Flow Connects the agent and the robot into one end-to-end process. See Lab 4. → Runs the agent, then the robot

One connected story across all four labs — the first three hand their output to the next through Data Service, and Maestro runs them as a single process.

docs.title: Authenticate with your tenant
docs.text:
You did this during Setup, but do it once more before you start Lab 1. Your login may have expired since then, and every lab writes to the same tenant.

uip login --authority https://cloud.uipath.com --organization tpenlabs -t CodingAgentsPractice

Verify you're pointed at the right place:

uip login status --output json

docs.title: Lab 1 — the Coded Agent
docs.text:
Jobs research + candidate matching

75 min build + 15 min review

docs.title: What's a Coded Agent?
docs.text:
Python agents that run on UiPath infrastructure. Not to be confused with the coding agent you're typing into — you write this one yourself.

You pick the framework, use the UiPath SDK, package it with one CLI command, and deploy it to Orchestrator.

SUPPORTED FRAMEWORKS LangGraph Graph-based, stateful agent flows LlamaIndex RAG and document-grounded agents OpenAI Agents SDK OpenAI's official agent framework Plain Python Simple function-based agents

docs.title: What the hiring agent does
docs.text:
The four nodes run in order — each one feeds the next, and Persist closes the loop by writing to Data Service for Lab 2 to pick up.

WHAT THE AGENT DOES Search 01 Web search for current openings in the target roles Generate 02 Structured job description: title, must-haves, nice-to-haves, level Match 03 Score the candidate pool against each job description Persist 04 Write jobs and matches to Data Service YOUR OBJECTIVES
  • 1 Prompt your coding agent to scaffold a LangGraph agent.
  • 2 Wire the WebSearch tool into the graph.
  • 3 Add a Data Service write step using the UiPath SDK.
  • 4 Run an eval set, then deploy to your tenant.
WHAT YOU NEED
  • A list of target job titles (for example, "RPA Developer", "AI Engineer").
  • candidates.csv — provided below, see The sample candidate data.
  • Your Anthropic or OpenAI API key.

docs.title: The prompt
docs.text:
This is real text you can paste:

Build a UiPath Coded Agent in LangGraph that:

1. Takes the name of a job as input
2. For each role, generates a structured JD with must-haves and nice-to-haves
3. Scores a list of candidates (generate the JSON list locally and use it as
   part of the solution; it should contain at least one profile for Forward
   Deployed Engineer) against each JD
4. Writes jobs and top-3 matches per role to the Data Service Jobs and
   Job Matches entities

Include an eval set with 5 cases. The name of the agent should be
{YourName}JobMatchingAgent. Use the UiPath SDK.
WHAT THE CODING AGENT DOES WITH THAT
  • 1 Loads the uipath-agents skill.
  • 2 Generates agent.py with four nodes.
  • 3 Builds Pydantic models for jobs and matches.
  • 4 Adds the Data Service write via the UiPath SDK.
  • 5 Creates evals/ with five cases.
  • 6 Asks you to review before publishing.

docs.title: What it generates
docs.text:
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph
from uipath import UiPath

sdk = UiPath()

def search_jobs(state):
    # Built-in WebSearch tool -> recent postings per role
    state["jobs"] = [web_search(t) for t in state["titles"]]
    return state

def generate_jd(state):
    # LLM call -> structured JD (Pydantic model)
    ...

def match_candidates(state):
    candidates = sdk.buckets.read("candidates.csv")
    # LLM scoring -> top-3 per role
    ...

def persist(state):
    sdk.entities.bulk_create("Jobs", state["jobs"])
    sdk.entities.bulk_create("JobMatches", state["matches"])

docs.title: Publish the agent
docs.text:
Your coding agent might ask what to do next

Once the agent is built and the evals pass, your coding agent might ask how you want to use the agent next — for example Studio Web, Local dev web server, or Skip. If you get this question, choose Local dev web server. It starts uip codedagent dev at http://localhost:8080, so you can try the agent in your browser. Nothing gets published at this step. Then come back here and publish the agent.

The dev server keeps running in the background. When it starts, your coding agent prints a link to the local dev console, for example:

Local dev console: http://localhost:8080/?token=<your-token>

Open that link in your browser to see your agent running and try it out. The token is unique to you and changes each time the dev server starts, so copy the full link from your own terminal — the one above won't work as is.

Here's what a run looks like in the local dev console: enter a job title in the input, click Execute, and watch the agent go through each step of the graph. When it finishes, the traces show each step and the output shows the ranked candidates.

Once the local dev server is running, your coding agent might offer to deploy the agent for you — to your personal workspace, the tenant feed, or a specific folder. If it does, ask it to deploy:

Deploy to tenant feed and create the process in CodingAgentsILT folder.

If your coding agent doesn't offer this, publish the agent with one of the two options below.

Both paths do the same thing. Run the commands yourself if you want to see each step, or hand the whole job to your coding agent.

ManuallyUsing Your Coding Agent

This assumes the uip CLI is installed and you're logged into the right org. Replace the project path and tenant name with your own.

# 1. Go to the agent project
cd job-matching-agent

# 2. Point the UiPath wrapper at the Python runtime
uip codedagent setup --force

# 3. Select the target tenant
uip login tenant set CodingAgentsPractice --output json
uip login status --output json

# 4. Initialize the coded agent project
uip codedagent init

# 5. Publish to the tenant feed
uip codedagent deploy --tenant

Give this prompt to your coding agent — it initializes the project and publishes for you:

Publish the {YourName}JobMatchingAgent coded agent I just built.

1. Point the UiPath wrapper at my Python runtime with `uip codedagent setup`.
2. Switch to the CodingAgentsPractice tenant and confirm `uip login status`
   shows the right org and tenant before going further.
3. Initialize the coded agent project, then publish it to the tenant feed.
4. Report back the package name and version you published, and stop if any
   step fails rather than retrying blindly.

Watch what it runs

The agent proposes each command before running it. Read them — publishing writes to your tenant feed, and that is the one step you want to see before it happens.

docs.title: Lab 2 — the RPA Workflow
docs.text: 75 min build + 15 min review

docs.title: Why RPA for this part?
docs.text: UiBank exposes registration only through a web form. There's no API. Some systems only have a UI — this is exactly what RPA was built for. RPA is the right tool Browser-based UI automation is faster and more reliable than scraping. Generated, not drawn You'll prompt your coding agent to build the XAML. No dragging activities onto a canvas. Connected to Lab 1 Read candidates from Data Service, write registration status back.

docs.title: What the workflow does
docs.text:
The four stages run in order — Read picks up what Lab 1 wrote, and Update hands the status on to the Coded App in Lab 3.

WHAT THE WORKFLOW DOES Read 01 Pull candidates from Data Service (matched in Lab 1) Loop 02 For each candidate, open the registration page Fill 03 Type each field, submit, wait for success Update 04 Write registration status back to Data Service YOUR OBJECTIVES
  • 1 Prompt your coding agent to generate the XAML workflow.
  • 2 Let it discover the project first, so it sees the existing packages.
  • 3 Review the generated workflow in Studio Desktop.
  • 4 Run against the sample CSV and verify the registrations.
Your target: uibank.uipath.com/register-account, the sample candidates.csv provided below, and UiPath Studio Desktop with the default packages.

docs.title: The sample candidate data
docs.text:
Download the file, or copy the text and save it as candidates.csv yourself. Both give you the same data.

Download the fileCopy the text

⬇️ Download candidates.csv

Save it in your workflow project folder.

Copy this and save it as candidates.csv in your workflow project folder:

first_name,last_name,middle_name,sex,title,employment_status,date_of_birth,marital_status,num_dependents,username,email,password
Alice,Nguyen,,Female,Ms,Full-time,1/15/1990,Single,0,alice.nguyen,alice.nguyen@example.com,Welcome2026!
Ben,Carter,J.,Male,Mr,Full-time,3/22/1985,Married,2,ben.carter,ben.carter@example.com,Welcome2026!
Clara,Osei,,Female,Ms,Full-time,7/4/1992,Single,1,clara.osei,clara.osei@example.com,Welcome2026!

Four things to tell the workflow about this data

  • An empty middle_name is valid. The form should skip the field, not type an empty string.
  • The date format is MM/DD/YYYY, which matches the form's picker.
  • UiBank rejects a username or email that's already registered. Everyone in the room starts from the same three candidates, and you'll run the workflow more than once, so the prompt asks the workflow to add _{YourName} and a timestamp to both.
  • All test passwords are demo-grade. In production, pull them from a vault.

docs.title: The prompt
docs.text:
Build a UiPath workflow that registers each candidate from candidates.csv at
uibank.uipath.com/register-account. The name of the workflow should be
{YourName}RegisterInUiBank. candidates.csv contains first_name, last_name,
middle_name, sex, title, employment_status, date_of_birth, marital_status,
num_dependents, username, email, and password. After each registration, write
the registration Status back to Data Service (Candidates entity).

UiBank doesn't allow two accounts with the same username or email, so make both
unique on every run: add _{YourName} and a timestamp to the username, and to
the part of the email before the @ (for example,
alice.nguyen_{YourName}_20261126153045 and
alice.nguyen_{YourName}_20261126153045@example.com).

Your coding agent might ask to install UiPath packages

If your project doesn't have the packages the workflow needs yet, your coding agent asks before it adds them — for example UiPath.UIAutomation.Activities to drive the browser form and UiPath.Excel.Activities to read candidates.csv. Confirm the install (choose Install both or the equivalent option). If you say no, the agent writes the workflow with placeholder selectors marked TODO Indicate, and you have to fix the targets in Studio yourself.

docs.title: How the workflow skill thinks
docs.text:
The uipath-rpa skill is discovery-first. It reads before it writes:

Let me inspect the project first...
  -> Reading project.json
  -> Found packages: UiPath.UIAutomation.Activities,
     UiPath.Excel.Activities, UiPath.WebAPI.Activities
  -> Inspected candidates.csv header

I'll create RegisterCandidates.xaml with:
  - Excel.ReadCsv -> DataTable
  - For Each Row in candidates
  - Open browser at registration URL
  - Type Into each form field (skip empty middle name)
  - Click Submit, wait for success element
  - Write Status back to Data Service (Candidates entity)
  - Try/Catch with screenshot on failure

Created RegisterCandidates.xaml (validated)

Four things worth noticing in that output:

Reads first 01 Discovers packages and CSV structure before writing any code. Picks the right activities 02 Knows Excel.ReadCsv exists and reaches for UI Automation activities. Handles edge cases 03 Empty middle name handled, screenshot on failure. Closes the loop 04 Writes status back to Data Service for the Coded App to read.

docs.title: Run it in Studio
docs.text:
Once your coding agent has generated the workflow, check that it really works before you move on:

  1. Open Studio Desktop.
  2. Open the project your coding agent created: {YourName}RegisterInUiBank. Your coding agent tells you where it saved it. In Studio, select Open and browse to the project's project.json.
  3. Run the workflow manually: select Debug File › Run File, or press Ctrl + F6.
  4. Watch the robot open uibank.uipath.com/register-account and fill in the form for each candidate in candidates.csv.

If the run fails

Copy the error message from Studio's Output panel and paste it into your coding agent. Ask it to fix the workflow, then run it again in Studio.

docs.title: Publish the workflow
docs.text:
Once the workflow runs in Studio, go back to your coding agent. It might ask whether to run the workflow itself or add more checks first. Ask it to publish instead:

Publish and create the process in CodingAgentsILT folder.

docs.title: Run it from Orchestrator
docs.text:
Once your coding agent confirms the process is created, run it from Orchestrator:

  1. Open Orchestrator and go to the CodingAgentsILT folder.
  2. Select Automations › Processes and find {YourName}RegisterInUiBank.
  3. Select Start a job (the ▶ icon) next to the process, then Start.
  4. Open the Jobs tab and watch the job until its state is Successful.

docs.title: Lab 3 — the Coded App
docs.text: 100 min build + 20 min review

docs.title: What's a Coded App?
docs.text: When the canvas-based UiPath Apps builder isn't enough. A custom web app in TypeScript and React — built in your IDE, governed by the platform. Your stack TypeScript, React, your design system, your favourite libraries. Platform access @uipath/uipath-typescript gives you Cases, Tasks, Processes, Entities, and Buckets. Enterprise-grade OAuth, IP restrictions, audit logs, and RBAC — all inherited from UiPath.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
A recruiter dashboard that reads the Jobs, Job Matches, and Candidates entities from Data Service.

WHAT THE DASHBOARD SHOWS
  • 1 Jobs list, sorted by recency.
  • 2 Click into any job for the full description.
  • 3 Candidate matches with their scores.
  • 4 Registration status badges.
  • 5 A button that triggers the Coded Agent on demand.

docs.title: The prompt
docs.text:
Build a Coded App using UiPath TypeScript SDK called recruiter-dashboard.
It should:

1. Read Jobs from the UiPath Data Service Jobs entity
2. For each job, show the JD and matched candidates
3. Show registration status from the Candidates entity
4. Add a button that triggers the Coded Agent

The name of the app should be {YourName}RecruiterApp. Use uipath-coded-apps
for the table component.

And the structure it generates:

recruiter-dashboard/
├── package.json
├── uipath.json
├── src/
│   ├── App.tsx
│   ├── pages/
│   │   ├── JobsList.tsx
│   │   └── JobDetail.tsx
│   ├── hooks/
│   │   ├── useJobs.ts
│   │   └── useCandidates.ts
│   └── api/uipath.ts
└── README.md

docs.title: What your coding agent reports back
docs.text:
After a few minutes your coding agent finishes with a summary of what it built and what it set up. Here's what to look for in it.

The tables The Candidates, Jobs, and Job Matches tabs use the UiPath DataTable widget from the coded apps tooling, with every column read-only. The matched candidates for a single job are built by hand, because the widget always loads a whole entity and can't filter it down to one job. The OAuth app The agent creates a public (non-confidential) OAuth app in your tenant called {YourName}RecruiterApp. It can read and write Data Service, start and monitor Orchestrator jobs, and redirects to http://localhost:5173. You don't have to create it by hand. The config Tenant details (org and tenant) go in uipath.json. The Data Service entity IDs and the agent's process name and folder go in src/config.ts. That's where to look if the app reads the wrong entity or triggers the wrong process.

Your OAuth app's client ID is yours alone

The summary shows the client ID of the OAuth app the agent created. Everyone gets a different one, so don't copy IDs from a neighbour's screen or from this page.

docs.title: Run the app locally
docs.text:
Start the app from the project folder:

cd recruiter-dashboard
npm run dev

Then open http://localhost:5173 and sign in with UiPath. Check that the Jobs, Job Matches, and Candidates tabs load data, and that the button triggers the Coded Agent.

Here's one example of what the app can look like: a form to run the Job Matching Agent, counters for jobs, matches, candidates, and registrations, and tabs with the Data Service records, including each candidate's registration status from Lab 2.

Your app will look different

Your coding agent designs the app from the prompt, so the layout, tabs, labels, and colours vary from participant to participant. That's expected. What matters is that it reads the Jobs, Job Matches, and Candidates entities, shows the registration status, and can trigger the Coded Agent.

docs.title: Deploy the app
docs.text:
Your coding agent usually stops after the build and asks before it packs, publishes, or deploys anything. When the app works locally, ask it to take it live:

Pack, publish, and deploy {YourName}RecruiterApp to the CodingAgentsILT folder.

Behind the scenes it runs three commands, the same ones you'd run yourself:

uip codedapp pack dist -n {YourName}RecruiterApp --version 1.0.0
uip codedapp publish
uip codedapp deploy --folder-key <CodingAgentsILT-folder-key>

The agent looks up the folder key for you. To find it yourself, run uip or folders list --output json and copy the key of the CodingAgentsILT folder.

Optional: a Register candidate button

Your {YourName}RegisterInUiBank process from Lab 2 is in the same CodingAgentsILT folder, so your coding agent may offer to add a Register candidate button next to each candidate. Say yes if you have time. The recruiter can then register a candidate straight from the dashboard.

docs.title: The Data Service hook
docs.text:
Here's how the dashboard reads jobs and matches:

import { UiPath } from '@uipath/uipath-typescript/core'
import { Entities } from '@uipath/uipath-typescript/entities'
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query'

const sdk = new UiPath({ /* env-based config */ })

export function useJobs() {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: ['jobs'],
    queryFn: async () => {
      const entities = new Entities(sdk)
      return entities.list('Jobs', { orderBy: 'createdAt desc' })
    },
  })
}

docs.title: 🔗 Lab 4 — the Maestro Flow
docs.text:
Agent → approval → robot, as one process

30 min build

Three pieces that work. Now make them run as one process. No walkthrough for this one — that's the point. You already have every skill you need.

Each lab left you with a deployed component and a Data Service entity. Maestro is what turns them into a single orchestrated process: it calls the agent, waits for the result, hands work to the RPA robot, and routes a human into the loop when one is needed.

YOUR OBJECTIVES
  • 1 Design a Maestro process that runs the three components end to end.
  • 2 Trigger the Coded Agent to research jobs and write matches to Data Service.
  • 3 Call the RPA workflow to register each matched candidate on UiBank.
  • 4 Surface the results in the Coded App so a recruiter can review them.
  • 5 Publish the process and run it once, start to finish.

docs.title: Which skill to use
docs.text: uipath-maestro-flow — it creates, validates, and debugs UiPath Flow projects in the .flow JSON format. You never hand-edit the JSON; you describe the process and let the agent build it, exactly as you did in the three labs.

docs.title: A prompt to start from
docs.text:
Treat this as a starting point, not a script. Read what the agent proposes, push back, and iterate.

Build a Maestro Flow called {YourName}RecruitmentPipeline that orchestrates the
three components I already deployed:

1. Start by running my {YourName}JobMatchingAgent coded agent, passing in a list
   of target job titles. Wait for it to finish writing Jobs and Job Matches to
   Data Service.
2. Then run my {YourName}RegisterInUiBank RPA process for the matched candidates,
   so each one gets registered on UiBank and the status is written back.
3. Add a human approval step before the RPA runs, so a recruiter can confirm
   the shortlist first.
4. Validate the flow, publish it, and tell me the process key.

Discover what's already deployed in my tenant before you start, and ask me
before creating anything new.

What 'done' looks like

One Maestro run that starts from a list of job titles and ends with registered candidates visible in your Coded App — with no manual step in between except the approval you designed in.

Stuck? That's expected

This is the part nobody walks you through. Ask your coding agent to explain what it generated, check the run in Orchestrator, and send the interesting failures our way with uip feedback send.

docs.title: Gotchas you'll hit
docs.text:
Things every team learns in the first month.

Gotcha What to do Trust but verify The agent is fast and confident. Always review generated XAML and run the eval set before publishing. Pin your skill versions Skills evolve. Lock to a version in your project so behaviour doesn't shift under you. Context window matters On large projects the agent can miss context. Tell it which files to focus on, or use an AGENTS.md. Auth before everything Run uip login first. Skills can't deploy if the CLI session expired — this is the usual cause of "it just stopped working".

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
One end-to-end recruitment pipeline, in four pieces:

# Component What it does 01 Coded Agent LangGraph agent. Searches the web for jobs, generates job descriptions, matches candidates, writes to Data Service. 02 RPA Workflow XAML workflow. Reads matched candidates, registers each on UiBank, updates status. 03 Coded App React dashboard. Shows jobs, matches, and registration status, with a trigger button. 04 Maestro Flow Runs the agent, waits for a recruiter's approval, then runs the RPA workflow.

All four talk to each other. All four were built with your coding agent. All in one IDE session.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
This week

  • Install the skills on your laptop and actually use them.
  • Extend your Maestro Flow — add another step, a second approval, or a schedule.

Next 30 days

  • Rebuild something you already maintain with a coding agent. Compare how long it took, and note where the agent needed correcting.
  • Write your own skill for a pattern your team repeats, so the agent gets it right without being told twice.
  • Push past the happy path: ask the agent for eval sets, error handling, and the deploy step you'd normally do by hand.

Ongoing

  • Bring your questions. No question is too basic, especially this early.
  • Tell us when something doesn't work. Run uip feedback send the moment a skill guesses wrong, a command fails, or a step takes three tries.
  • Say what you'd want next. The rough edges you report are what shape the next version of the skills and the CLI.

Everything you install before the workshop starts. Work through it top to bottom — each section verifies itself before you move on.

Do this before the session

Training Environment

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Node.js (LTS) — required for the UiPath CLI and the React app build.

  1. Download the LTS version from nodejs.org
  2. Verify with node --version and npm --version

npm version must be 11.x.x

If npm --version returns a different version, upgrade it:

WindowsMac 
npm install --global npm@11

npm install -g npm@11

Python 3.10+ — required for coded agents.

  1. Download from python.org/downloads — on Windows, check Add Python to PATH during install
  2. Verify with python --version or python3 --version

.NET SDK 8.0 — required to build and run UiPath Studio projects.

  1. Download from dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/8.0 — or on Mac, install via Homebrew: 
    brew install --cask dotnet-sdk
  2. Verify with dotnet --list-sdks — you should see 8.x.x in the output

Windows — make sure .NET is on your PATH

If dotnet is not recognised after install, add it to the PATH manually in PowerShell: 

$env:Path = "C:\Program Files\dotnet;$env:Path"
dotnet --list-sdks

UiPath Studio — required to open, run, and debug generated XAML workflows. Currently supported on Windows only; Mac support is coming soon.

  1. Download from uipath.com/start-trial
  2. Sign in with your UiPath account and verify Studio launches

Git — required for the UiPath skills marketplace. Try Method 1 first; if it doesn't work, use Method 2.

Method 1: winget (quickest)Method 2: Download the installer
  1. Open a terminal and run: 
    winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget
  2. If prompted to accept terms, type Y and press Enter.
  3. Wait for "Successfully installed", then close the window.
  1. Go to git-scm.com/download/win — the 64-bit installer should download automatically.
  2. Run the downloaded file (e.g. Git-2.xx.x-64-bit.exe). Click Yes if Windows asks for admin permission.
  3. Click through the installer accepting all defaults. On the "Adjusting your PATH environment" screen, make sure the middle option is selected: "Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software" — this is the default.
  4. Click Finish when done.

Required for both methods

PATH changes only take effect in new windows. Close every open terminal, then open a fresh Command Prompt and verify: 

git --version
You should see something like git version 2.45.1.windows.1.

docs.title: 2. Install a Coding Agent
docs.text:
Pick one — or install both:

# Claude Code (Anthropic)
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

# Codex CLI (OpenAI)
npm install -g @openai/codex

Verify: claude --version or codex --version

Claude Code installation error?

If the install fails with a scripts permission error, run: 

npm config set allow-scripts=@anthropic-ai/claude-code --location=user
Then run the install command again: 
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

npm permission errors on Mac?

A global install without write permissions is the usual cause. Point npm at a folder you own: 

mkdir -p ~/.npm-global
npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

docs.title: 3. Install the UiPath CLI
docs.text:
npm install -g @uipath/cli@latest

Verify: uip --version — you should see 1.195.1 or later.

docs.title: 4. Install UiPath Skills into Your Coding Agent
docs.text:
Claude CodeCodex 
# 1. Add the marketplace (once)
claude plugin marketplace add https://github.com/UiPath/skills
# 2. Install the plugin from it
claude plugin install uipath@uipath-marketplace
uip skills install

# 1. Add the marketplace (once)
codex plugin marketplace add UiPath/skills --ref main
uip skills install

Confirm these four skills appear in the output — the exercises rely on them:

  • uipath-rpa — Studio XAML workflows
  • uipath-agents — Python coded agents

What each skill actually knows

See What's a Coding Agent? for the full skill catalog and how skills get discovered.

docs.title: 5. Install the Coded Apps Tool
docs.text:
The Coded Apps skill requires an additional CLI tool:

uip tools install @uipath/codedapp-tool

Verify the tool is available:

uip tools list

docs.title: 6. Authenticate with Your Tenant
docs.text:
uip login --authority https://cloud.uipath.com --organization tpenlabs -t CodingAgentsPractice

Verify you're pointed at the right place:

uip login status --output json

docs.title: 7. Open Your Project and Start a Session
docs.text:
cd my-project && claude
# or
cd my-project && codex

Skills are auto-discovered on session start. Ask the agent to build a coded agent and it will load the right skill automatically.

You're set up

Node.js, Python, .NET, Studio, Git, a coding agent, the uip CLI, the UiPath skills, and an authenticated tenant. Time to build something.

docs.title: What's a Coding Agent?
docs.text:
Learn how coding agents work and what makes them useful for UiPath automation work.

A coding agent is an AI assistant that reads, writes, and reasons about code — not just autocompletes it. Instead of suggesting the next line, it understands a goal described in plain English, explores the codebase, makes decisions, and generates entire working components. You stay in control: you review what it builds, ask it to adjust, and iterate until it's right.

Several coding agents are available today, each with their own strengths:

  • Claude Code — Anthropic's CLI-based agent, runs in your terminal, deeply integrated with the file system. This is the one used in this exercise.
  • Codex CLI — OpenAI's command-line coding agent, similar terminal-first approach
  • Cursor — an IDE built around AI, tight editor integration with inline generation and multi-file context
  • Gemini CLI — Google's terminal agent, strong on reasoning and long context
  • GitHub Copilot Agent — embedded in VS Code and JetBrains, well suited for in-editor workflows

What makes coding agents especially powerful for UiPath work is the skill layer: by loading domain-specific knowledge about UiPath activities, APIs, and project conventions, the agent can generate production-ready automation code — not generic boilerplate. That's exactly what the UiPath skills in this exercise do.

docs.title: The Mental Model
docs.text:
Five concepts show up in every coding agent:

Concept What it is Tools Built-in actions the agent can take: read a file, run a bash command, search the web, edit code, etc. Skills Domain knowledge bundles the agent loads when it sees a matching task. Like a playbook for one thing. Commands Manual shortcuts you type: /commit, /test, /deploy. Triggered by you, not the agent. Hooks Run automatically at lifecycle events: before an edit, after a commit, on session start. Used for guardrails. Subagents Specialised workers spawned by the main agent. Used to parallelise or isolate complex tasks.

Plugins

A plugin is a package that bundles any of these together — like a Marketplace app for your coding agent. The UiPath skills used in this exercise are plugins.

docs.title: Tools, in practice
docs.text:
Claude Code's built-in tools are always available — no setup required:

Tool What it does Read Read any file in your project Edit / Write Modify or create files Bash Execute shell commands Glob / Grep Search across the codebase WebSearch / WebFetch Look things up online Task Spawn a subagent

Extension Tools (MCP)

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard way to give your coding agent new tools without changing the agent itself.

  • GitHub MCP — read issues, open PRs
  • Atlassian MCP — Jira, Confluence
  • Slack MCP — read channels, post messages
  • Custom UiPath MCP — call Orchestrator, Maestro

docs.title: Skills, in practice
docs.text:
A skill is a folder — sitting in .claude/skills/ (or equivalent), with a SKILL.md inside.

Property What it means Discovered automatically The agent reads each SKILL.md's description. When your prompt matches, it loads the full skill on demand. More than just text Skills can bundle reference docs, code patterns, helper scripts, even compiled binaries the agent can run. Scoped permissions A skill declares which tools it's allowed to use. Bash access can be tightly controlled.

docs.title: What's in a SKILL.md file
docs.text:
Every skill is built around a single SKILL.md file. Here's what one looks like:

---
name: uipath-coded-agents
description: Scaffold, build, run, evaluate, and deploy UiPath coded agents...
allowed-tools: [Read, Edit, Bash(uip:*), Bash(uipath:*)]
---

# How to build a UiPath coded agent

When the user asks for a new coded agent:

1. Run `uipath new --framework langgraph`
2. Create agent.py following the pattern in references/
3. Add an evals/ folder with at least 5 test cases
4. Run `uipath eval` before deploying

## References
- references/sdk-methods.md
- references/langgraph-patterns.md

The file has four parts:

Part What it does Frontmatter Declares the skill's name, description, and which tools it's allowed to use. Discovery prompt The description field is what the agent matches against your request — this is how the skill gets loaded automatically. Instructions The body of the file: a step-by-step prompt the agent follows when the skill is active. References Paths to files in the skill folder the agent can read for deeper context — API docs, code patterns, example projects.

docs.title: Where UiPath fits in this picture
docs.text:
UiPath ships a plugin for Claude Code. It bundles skills, hooks, and references — giving the agent domain knowledge about UiPath products out of the box.

npm -g install @uipath/cli
uip skills install

The plugin contains three things:

What Details 10+ skills Domain knowledge for every UiPath product: uipath-agents, uipath-coded-apps, uipath-rpa, uipath-maestro-flow, uipath-platform, uipath-test, and more. 1 subagent uipath-project-discovery-agent — auto-runs on first contact with a UiPath project and builds context for the agent. Hooks & references Session-start nudges, activity docs, and allowlists for safe read-only commands.

docs.title: The UiPath skill catalog
docs.text:
The plugin includes skills for every part of the UiPath platform. Three of them drive the labs in this exercise:

Skill Description uipath-agents Scaffold, build, run, evaluate, and deploy coded agents (LangGraph, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Agents) uipath-rpa Generate and edit RPA workflows (XAML) for Studio Desktop with a discovery-first approach uipath-coded-apps Push/pull TypeScript + React apps to Studio Web, pack & publish to Orchestrator uipath-solution Create and deploy solutions uipath-maestro-flow Create, validate, and debug UiPath Flow projects using the .flow JSON format uipath-platform Auth, Orchestrator management, solution lifecycle, Integration Service, CLI tools uipath-test Generate, run, and maintain automated test suites for UiPath projects

Skills used in this exercise

The three skills in bold — uipath-agents, uipath-rpa, and uipath-coded-apps — are the ones you'll use to build the loan underwriting pipeline.

Maestro ties the labs together

The first three labs each give you a working piece: an agent, a workflow, and an app. The Maestro lab wires the agent and the workflow into a single orchestrated process, so one run goes from job titles to registered candidates you can see in the app.
